name: The paths of the Gītā: action, knowledge, meditation and devotion

definitions.definition: The Gītā names two ancient paths, knowledge for the Sāṃkhyas and action for the yogins (3.3), holds them one in result (5.4–5), adds meditation (ch. 6) and devotion (chs. 7–12), and states that some see the self by meditation, some by Sāṃkhya, some by action, and some by worship after hearing (13.24–25). Commentators rank them differently (see dsp:gita-primary-teaching).

relations.note: devotion is one of the Gītā's paths and, for the Vaiṣṇava readers, their culmination

name: Action without attachment to its fruit (niṣkāma karma)

definitions.definition: Acting as duty, with evenness, abandoning attachment and the fruit, offering the act to the Lord; action so done does not bind (BhG 2.47–48, 3.19, 4.20, 9.27–28, 18.6).
Yudhiṣṭhira's dharma practised 'not for the fruit of dharma' (MBh 3.32.4).

The duty arising from one's own nature and station, to be done even if imperfect in preference to another's (BhG 3.35, 18.47); by it, as worship of the Lord, one reaches perfection (18.46); the meat-seller holds his inherited work as his dharma (MBh 3.198).

One who has given up the desires of the mind and is content in the self, unagitated in sorrow and pleasure, senses withdrawn, awake where beings sleep, unmoved as the ocean, in the brāhmī state (BhG 2.54–72); with close parallels in the devotee dear to the Lord (12.13–20) and the one beyond the guṇas (14.22–25).

relations.note: the description is of one liberated in this life as the Advaita commentators read it; the Gītā itself does not use 'jīvanmukti'

name: The field and the knower of the field (kṣetra–kṣetrajña)

definitions.definition: The body and all of prakṛti with its modifications is the field; the one who knows it is its knower; the Lord is the knower in all fields; knowledge of both is true knowledge (BhG 13.1–6, 13.33–34).
Vāsudeva is the knower of the field (MBh 12.326.38).

relations.note: the knower of the field corresponds to the Mokṣadharma's twenty-fifth ('the knower is the twenty-fifth', 12.294.38)

name: The three guṇas

definitions.definition: Sattva, rajas and tamas, born of prakṛti, bind the embodied one — sattva by attachment to happiness and knowledge, rajas to action, tamas by negligence, sloth and sleep (BhG 14.5–8); each prevails by overpowering the others; their signs, destinies and the classification of faith, food, austerity, giving, knowledge, action, agent, intellect, steadfastness and happiness (chs. 14, 17, 18); no being is free of them (18.40).

notes: U05's contribution; classical Sāṃkhya's account is given by U09.

name: The two natures of the Lord (aparā and parā prakṛti)

definitions.definition: The Lord's lower nature is eightfold — earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect, ego — and his higher nature is the life-element that upholds the world; both are the womb of all beings (BhG 7.4–6); he sends forth beings resting on his prakṛti (9.8).

members: aparā prakṛti: earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect, ego

name: The Lord's descent (avatāra / prādurbhāva)

definitions.definition: Though unborn, the Lord comes into being by his own māyā whenever dharma declines, to protect the good, destroy evil-doers and establish dharma (BhG 4.6–8); knowing his divine birth frees one (4.9).
Nārāyaṇa's successive manifestations: Varāha, Narasiṃha, Vāmana, Rāma Bhārgava, Rāma Dāśarathi, the appearance at Mathurā; earlier the Swan and Hayaśiras (MBh 12.326.72–94).

notes: No fixed list of ten appears in the critical text of the Nārāyaṇīya; Kalki is not named there.

definitions.definition: The sovereign form shown to Arjuna by grace through a divine eye: the whole universe in one body, as bright as a thousand suns, and as Time devouring the warriors (BhG 11.5–34); seen only by undivided devotion (11.52–54); a similar self-manifestation occurs in the Kaurava court (MBh 5.129) and Mārkaṇḍeya sees the worlds within a divine child (3.186).

The Lord as the best in each class — among lights the sun, among words Oṃ, among sacrifices japa, among sages Vyāsa, and so on — every glory springing from a fragment of his splendour; he sustains the world with one fragment (BhG ch. 10; 7.8–11).

The Gītā keeps the wheel of sacrifice between gods and men (3.10–16) but widens sacrifice to austerity, yoga, study, sense-restraint, breath and knowledge (4.25–30), declares the sacrifice of knowledge highest (4.33) and sees offering, oblation, fire and offerer as Brahman (4.24); sacrifice is to be done without desire for fruit (17.11; 18.5); the Anugītā describes an inner sacrifice of the senses (14.20).

Saṃnyāsa is laying aside desire-prompted actions, tyāga relinquishing the fruit of all actions (BhG 18.2); obligatory acts of sacrifice, giving and austerity are not to be abandoned (18.5); relinquishment is threefold by the guṇas (18.7–9); the true renouncer is the one who acts without depending on the fruit (6.1).
Faith born of one's nature is sāttvic, rājasic or tāmasic, accordingly worshipping gods, yakṣas and rākṣasas, or ghosts and spirits; a person is made of faith (BhG 17.2–4).

Sāttvic food increases life, vitality, strength, health and happiness and is savoury and wholesome; rājasic food is bitter, sour, salty, hot and burning and brings pain and disease; tāmasic food is stale, tasteless, putrid, leftover and impure (BhG 17.7–10).

name: The threefold austerity (tapas) of body, speech and mind

definitions.definition: Austerity of body (worship of gods, the twice-born, teachers and the wise; purity, uprightness, celibacy, non-harm), of speech (non-agitating, truthful, pleasant, beneficial speech and recitation) and of mind (serenity, gentleness, silence, self-restraint, purity of being); each again sāttvic, rājasic or tāmasic (BhG 17.14–19); self-tormenting austerity not enjoined by scripture is demonic (17.5–6).

Giving because it ought to be given, to one who makes no return, at the right place and time to the worthy, is sāttvic; for a return or grudgingly, rājasic; at the wrong place and time, to the unworthy, with contempt, tāmasic (BhG 17.20–22).

name: The guṇa-classification of knowledge, action, agent, intellect, steadfastness and happiness

definitions.definition: Knowledge, action, agent, intellect (buddhi), steadfastness (dhṛti) and happiness are each sāttvic, rājasic or tāmasic (BhG 18.19–39) — sāttvic knowledge seeing one imperishable being in all, sāttvic happiness 'poison at first, nectar at the end'.

name: The divine and demonic endowments (daivī and āsurī sampad)

definitions.definition: Two kinds of beings: the divine endowment (fearlessness, purity, non-harm, truth, compassion and the rest) leads to liberation; the demonic (hypocrisy, pride, anger, harshness, ignorance) to bondage; the demonic deny a Lord and live for desire (BhG ch. 16).

name: The inverted aśvattha tree of saṃsāra

definitions.definition: The world-tree with roots above and branches below, whose leaves are the Vedic hymns, nourished by the guṇas, binding through action, to be cut with the axe of non-attachment (BhG 15.1–4); the Anugītā's tree of Brahman (14.47).

name: The perishable, the imperishable and the highest person

definitions.definition: The perishable (all beings), the imperishable (the unchanging) and the highest person (Puruṣottama) beyond both, who sustains the three worlds (BhG 15.16–18).

relations.note: the Gītā's three persons and the Mokṣadharma's 24/25/26 both set a supreme above the knower of prakṛti

definitions.definition: Whatever state one remembers when leaving the body, to that one goes, having been absorbed in it; so one should remember the Lord at all times (BhG 8.5–7); the guṇa prevailing at death determines the next birth (14.14–15).

name: The two paths after death (bright and dark)

definitions.definition: The bright path (fire, light, day, bright fortnight, northern course) leads knowers of Brahman to non-return; the dark path (smoke, night, dark fortnight, southern course) to the lunar light and return (BhG 8.23–26); Bhīṣma waits for the northern course to die (MBh 6.114).

notes: U05's contribution; the Upaniṣadic doctrine is covered by U03.

name: The day and night of Brahmā

definitions.definition: Brahmā's day and night each last a thousand ages; at day beings emerge from the unmanifest and at night dissolve into it, again and again (BhG 8.17–19); at the end of a kalpa beings enter the Lord's prakṛti (9.7).
The afflicted, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth and the knower worship the Lord; the knower is the best and is the Lord's very self (BhG 7.16–18).

name: Devotion (bhakti)

definitions.definition: Devotion to the Lord: accepting a leaf or flower offered with love (BhG 9.26), bearing the devotee's welfare (9.22), making even the wicked righteous (9.30), the means by which he is seen and entered (11.54), preferred over worship of the unmanifest as easier (12.2–5), attained in its supreme form by one who has become Brahman (18.54).
Exclusive devotion (ekānta-bhakti) to Nārāyaṇa, the highest dharma, by which the ekāntins enter Vāsudeva directly (MBh 12.336.3–4, 12.332.18).

notes: U05's contribution (the Gītā and Nārāyaṇīya); later bhakti theory is given by U16 and U25.

definitions.definition: By the Lord's grace the devotee attains the eternal abode even while acting (BhG 18.56, 18.62), crosses all obstacles (18.58), sees the universal form (11.47), and is lifted from the ocean of saṃsāra (12.7); the Lord dwelling in the heart destroys the darkness of ignorance (10.11).
Taking refuge in the Lord alone, who frees from all sins (BhG 18.66); those who take refuge cross his māyā (7.14); Rāma protects anyone who comes once for refuge (Rāmāyaṇa 6.18.33).

The wise act unattached for the welfare and cohesion of the world, as Janaka did and as the Lord himself acts though he has nothing to gain, without unsettling the understanding of the ignorant (BhG 3.20–26).

In the Gītā: brahmanirvāṇa (2.72, 5.24–26), non-return (8.15–16), entering the Lord after knowing him by devotion (18.55), freedom from birth, death and old age beyond the guṇas (14.20); in the Mokṣadharma: the twenty-fifth becoming alone (kevala) on awakening and attaining the state of the twenty-sixth (12.294, 12.296).
Entry through the sun and the vyūhas into Vāsudeva, the ekāntins entering him directly (MBh 12.332.13–18).

name: Liberation while living

definitions.definition: The Gītā speaks of creation conquered 'even here' by those established in sameness (5.19), of brahmanirvāṇa near on every side for self-knowers (5.26), and of the one of steady wisdom and the one beyond the guṇas; Janaka claims freedom while ruling (MBh 12.17.18) and Sulabhā tests the claim (12.308).

notes: The word 'jīvanmukta' is later; see U13 for the Advaita concept.

definitions.definition: The embodied self (ātman, dehin) is unborn, eternal, not slain when the body is slain, passing into new bodies as into new clothes, unmanifest and unthinkable (BhG 2.11–30); the knower of the field (13.1–2); an eternal portion of the Lord (15.7); Bhṛgu defends the existence of a living self in the elemental body (MBh 12.175–185).

name: The hierarchy of senses, mind and intellect

definitions.definition: The senses are high, the mind higher, the intellect higher still, and beyond the intellect is 'he' (BhG 3.42); the body as chariot with mind as charioteer, senses as horses, understanding as reins (MBh 11.7.13).
The way of action is deep: one must know action, wrong action and inaction, and see inaction in action and action in inaction (BhG 4.16–18); actions burnt in the fire of knowledge (4.19, 4.37).

name: The fate of the one fallen from yoga

definitions.definition: One who falls from yoga is not lost: he dwells in the worlds of the meritorious, is reborn among the pure and prosperous or in a family of yogins, recovers his former understanding and, perfected through many births, reaches the highest goal (BhG 6.37–45).

name: The varṇas by guṇa and action

definitions.definition: The fourfold order is created by the Lord according to guṇa and action (BhG 4.13), each varṇa's duties arising from its nature (18.41–44); yet the epic also teaches that varṇa arose from actions in a world wholly of Brahman (MBh 12.181.10) and that conduct makes the brāhmaṇa (3.177.16); service is the śūdra's dharma (12.60.27–28).

notes: See dsp:varna-by-birth-or-conduct-epic for the recorded tension.

name: The twenty-four principles (epic Sāṃkhya)

definitions.definition: The Sāṃkhyas enumerate twenty-four principles together with prakṛti (the unmanifest), the twenty-fifth being beyond them (MBh 12.294.42); the Gītā's field lists the great elements, ego, intellect, the unmanifest, the ten organs and mind, and the five objects (BhG 13.5).

notes: The epic's lists vary between dialogues (e.g. 'eight prakṛtis and sixteen modifications'); the member list here follows BhG 13.5.

definitions.definition: The twenty-fifth is the knower, the self that is 'awakening' (budhyamāna), which on knowing itself becomes alone; the twenty-sixth is the ever-awakened (buddha), stainless and eternal, which the twenty-fifth does not know until it awakens to it and attains its state (MBh 12.294.43, 12.296.7–12; Yājñavalkya 12.306).

name: The distinction of sattva (intellect) and the knower of the field

definitions.definition: Sattva and the knower of the field are different yet joined, like fish and water, the gnat and the udumbara fruit, the reed and the muñja grass (MBh 12.187.39; 12.240.21–22).
Bhīṣma's fourfold dhyāna-yoga; in the first meditation reflection, reasoning and discrimination arise (MBh 12.188.1, 12.188.15), and the persevering sage reaches the happiness of nirvāṇa.

name: The fourfold form of the Lord (the vyūhas)

definitions.definition: Vāsudeva (the knower of the field), Saṃkarṣaṇa (the jīva), Pradyumna (mind) and Aniruddha (ego, source of Brahmā), each arising from the prior; the liberated pass back through them into Vāsudeva (MBh 12.326.38, 12.326.68–69, 12.327.26, 12.332.13–18).

relations.note: the vyūhas are correlated with jīva, mind and ego in the Nārāyaṇīya

name: The dharma of the one-pointed (ekāntika / sātvata dharma)

definitions.definition: Exclusive devotion to Nārāyaṇa, practised by the ekāntins — non-violent, knowing the self, delighting in the welfare of beings — the best dharma, equal to Sāṃkhya-yoga, taught to Arjuna before the battle, handed down from the beginning of the Kṛta age (MBh 12.336).
The island north of the milk ocean where the white, one-pointed devotees dwell and Nārāyaṇa reveals himself (MBh 12.323.23–26; Nārada's visit 12.321–326).

name: The five systems of knowledge (Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pañcarātra, Veda, Pāśupata)

definitions.definition: Five systems holding different views, proclaimed by Kapila, Hiraṇyagarbha, the Lord himself, Apāntaratamas and Śiva respectively, in all of which Nārāyaṇa is the culmination (MBh 12.337.59–67).

name: Dharma and the aims of life (trivarga, puruṣārtha)

definitions.definition: Dharma, artha, kāma and mokṣa, all treated in the epic (MBh 1.56.33); dharma is the source of artha and kāma (18.5.49); Rāma asks Bharata whether he pursues each at its time (Rāmāyaṇa 2.100).

notes: U05's contribution; the Dharmaśāstra account is given by U02.

name: The stages of life (āśrama)

definitions.definition: Bhṛgu teaches the four āśramas (MBh 12.184); Yudhiṣṭhira's wish to renounce is answered with arguments for the householder's and king's stage (12.7–36); Janaka teaches Śuka that the āśramas are to be passed in order, though one already free may renounce (12.312–313); the son urges seeking the self without delay (12.169).

notes: U05's contribution; the Dharmaśāstra account is given by U02.

definitions.definition: Dharma is hard to know: the hunter Balāka reaches heaven, the truth-telling Kauśika hell (MBh 8.49); the golden rule is its summary (13.114.8; 5.39.57); in distress other rules apply (12.139); the vulgate Yakṣapraśna says its truth is hidden in a cave.

'I am Time, the destroyer of worlds' (BhG 11.32); 'Time takes all and gives all' (MBh 12.217.25); in Vidura's parable time is the serpent, days and nights the rats (11.5–6); all accumulations end in exhaustion (Rāmāyaṇa 2.105.16).

name: Fate and human effort (daiva and puruṣakāra)

definitions.definition: Several causes are debated: nature (svabhāva, Prahlāda 12.215), time (Bali 12.217), fate (daiva), human effort (Draupadī 3.28–33) and karma (Gautamī 13.1); the Gītā counts daiva as the fifth of five causes of action (18.14), and Bhīṣma teaches that fate does not bear fruit without effort (13.6.7).

Called the highest dharma (MBh 1.11.12; 13.116; 3.297.55); taught by Tulādhāra (12.253–256), Vicakhnu (12.257) and Vidura (5.33.48); the meat-seller notes that no one lives without harm (3.199); the kṣatriya's righteous war is his own dharma (BhG 2.31).
The ekāntins are non-violent; the Lord is worshipped by sacrifice without slaughter (MBh 12.336; 12.323–324).
The Rāmāyaṇa's Rāma, 'dharma in bodily form' (3.37.13), keeps his father's word as dharma (2.21.40), holds truth as the lord of the world (2.109.13), and teaches the duties of kingship (2.100).

name: The dharma of the devoted wife (pativratā)

definitions.definition: The devoted wife's service of her husband as a deity gives her power over an angry ascetic (MBh 3.196–197) and over death (Sāvitrī, 3.281); Anasūyā teaches it to Sītā (Rāmāyaṇa 2.117–119); Umā expounds women's dharma (MBh 13.126–134).

The king protects the people by the science of punishment first composed by Brahmā (MBh 12.59); Rāma's questions to Bharata on counsel, treasury, army and the aims of life (Rāmāyaṇa 2.100); the debate on capital punishment (MBh 12.259).
In extremity the rules may be set aside to preserve life, with later expiation, as in Viśvāmitra's taking the dog's haunch (MBh 12.139).

name: Teacher, transmission and secrecy in the Gītā and epic

definitions.definition: The yoga was handed down from Vivasvat to Manu to Ikṣvāku and the royal sages, then lost and taught again (BhG 4.1–3); Arjuna becomes a disciple (2.7); knowledge is learned from seers of truth by prostration, inquiry and service (4.34); it is not to be told to one without austerity or devotion (18.67); Sañjaya heard it by Vyāsa's grace (18.75); after instruction the disciple decides (18.63); Kṛṣṇa cannot repeat it (Anugītā 14.16.11); knowledge may be received even from a śūdra (MBh 12.306.85), yet Vidura, of śūdra birth, defers to Sanatsujāta (5.41.5).

name: Yogic powers in the epic

definitions.definition: Yogins with yoga-power enter other beings at will (MBh 12.289.24); Sulabhā enters Janaka's mind (12.308); Jaigīṣavya moves unseen between the worlds (9.49); Vidura enters Yudhiṣṭhira's body at death (15.33.25); Śuka rises into the sky (12.318–320).

notes: The epic's warnings: the path of yoga is hard and dangerous (12.289, low confidence on the exact images); the Gītā warns against self-tormenting austerities (17.5–6).

definitions.definition: A sight granted by the Lord or a seer: Kṛṣṇa gives Arjuna a divine eye to see the universal form (BhG 11.8); Vyāsa gives Sañjaya sight of the whole war (MBh 6.2; BhG 18.75).

name: Oṃ

definitions.definition: The one-syllabled Brahman to be uttered at death (BhG 8.13), the praṇava in all the Vedas (7.8), the first word of 'oṃ tat sat' with which rites begin (17.23–24), 'among words the one syllable' (10.25).

notes: U05's contribution; the Upaniṣadic and mantra-śāstra accounts are given by U03 and U31.

definitions.definition: At death the yogin fixes the breath between the brows (BhG 8.10) or, closing the gates and holding the mind in the heart and the breath in the head, utters Oṃ remembering the Lord (8.12–13); Bhīṣma chooses his time and his self breaks through the crown (MBh 6.114; 13.154.5); Vidura enters Yudhiṣṭhira (15.33.25); Śuka rises by yoga (12.318–320).

The four ages and dharma's decline through them (MBh 3.148; Vyāsa to Śuka 12.224); the Lord's coming age after age (BhG 4.8); Mārkaṇḍeya's vision of the dissolution (3.186); in the Rāmāyaṇa, Nārada ties austerity by each varṇa to the ages (7.74).

name: The virtues called knowledge (BhG 13.7–11)

definitions.definition: Absence of pride and pretence, non-harm, patience, uprightness, service of the teacher, purity, steadiness, self-control, dispassion, absence of ego, seeing the evil of birth, death, age, disease and pain, non-attachment, evenness, unswerving devotion, love of solitude, constancy in self-knowledge and insight into the goal of truth — these are called knowledge (BhG 13.7–11).

notes: Commentators count the items as twenty; the count is not in the text.

name: The Lord in the heart of all beings

definitions.definition: The Lord dwells in the heart of all beings, moving them by his māyā (BhG 18.61); he is the self seated in the heart of all (10.20), the source of memory and knowledge (15.15), seated in the heart of all as the light of lights (13.17), and dwelling in his devotees' hearts destroys their darkness (10.11).

Evenness in success and failure is yoga (BhG 2.48); the wise see the same in all (5.18) and 'even here' conquer creation (5.19); the yogin sees the self in all (6.29) and others' pleasure and pain as his own (6.32); Jaigīṣavya is unmoved by praise and blame (MBh 12.222).
